title: Vegan Full English
subtitle: Tofu scramble, vegan sausages, roasted tomatoes, and mushrooms
excerpt: All the architecture of a full English, roasted tomatoes, golden mushrooms, baked beans, and a savoury tofu scramble, without any animal products.
sourceNotes: Developed from modern plant-based cooking conventions. The tofu scramble technique uses turmeric and black salt (kala namak) for colour and an egg-like flavour, though both are optional.

recipe.temperatureNote: Oven temperature for roasting tomatoes and mushrooms

To add a small amount of liquid to a hot pan after frying, loosening the caramelised residue from the base and incorporating it into a sauce or mixture.

content.text: A vegan full English has the same logic as the original: a mixture of textures and flavours on one plate that adds up to more than the sum of its parts. The tofu scramble is the centrepiece, and it works best when you press the tofu dry, season it boldly, and let it sit undisturbed long enough to get some colour. The roasted tomatoes and golden mushrooms cook in the oven while you handle the scramble, so the timing is straightforward once you know the order.
What you need

For the tofu scramble you will also need 300 g firm tofu (pressed dry and crumbled), 1 tsp ground turmeric, 1 tbsp nutritional yeast, a pinch of black salt (kala namak, optional but it gives an eggy flavour), and 1 small garlic clove, finely chopped. Vegan sausages can be cooked in the oven at the same time. Follow the packet instructions for timing.
Roast the tomatoes and mushrooms
Heat the oven to 200 °C. Place the
tomato
halves cut-side up and the
mushrooms-portobello

gill-side up on the baking tray. Drizzle with 15 ml of the olive oil and season with salt and pepper. Roast for 18 to 20 minutes until the tomatoes have softened and the mushrooms are tender and juicy. Add any vegan sausages to the tray at the same time, following the packet cooking time.
Make the tofu scramble

While the oven items cook, press the tofu dry between sheets of kitchen paper, pressing firmly to remove as much moisture as possible. Crumble it into rough chunks, not too fine, you want some texture. Set the large frying pan over medium-high heat with the remaining 15 ml olive oil. Add the tofu and spread it out in a single layer. Do not stir for 3 minutes, let it sit and develop colour on the underside.
Once it has some golden spots, add the garlic and
scramble
everything together with a silicone spatula. Sprinkle over the turmeric and nutritional yeast and stir through. Add a splash of water to
deglaze
any stuck bits. Cook for a further 2 minutes, stirring occasionally. Season well with salt, if using kala namak (black salt), add it now for that sulphurous, eggy quality. Taste and adjust.
Warm the beans and build the plate
Warm the
baked-beans

in a small pan over low heat. Arrange everything on two warm plates: scramble in the centre, mushroom and tomato alongside, sausages to one side, and beans poured over or kept separate. Thick toast is the natural accompaniment, made from sourdough or a good white sandwich loaf.
Troubleshooter

Tofu scramble is wet and pale: the tofu wasn't pressed dry enough, or the heat was too low. Press more aggressively, wrap in a clean tea towel and stand a heavy pan on top for 5 minutes. A properly hot pan and patience on the first side will give you colour.

Scramble tastes bland: tofu is the most neutral ingredient in the recipe and needs bold seasoning. Nutritional yeast adds depth, turmeric adds colour and earthiness, and kala namak adds that characteristic egg flavour. Be generous with salt.
Where this dish lives

The vegan full English has become a staple of café culture in Britain over the past decade, appearing on brunch menus from Brighton to Edinburgh. It doesn't try to be a perfect replica of the original. The textures and flavours are their own thing, but it delivers the same sense of a substantial, varied breakfast that feels like an occasion rather than a quick bowl of cereal. Black salt (kala namak) is the one ingredient that bridges the gap well. It's worth ordering online if you can't find it locally.
